chapter.title: Introduction
chapter.para: ooRexx/.NET connects two runtimes that run in the same process: an ooRexx interpreter and the .NET runtime (the CLR). Each side sees the other's objects as its own, by reference: nothing is copied but the simplest values (strings, numbers, logical values), and a message sent to a proxy reaches the object on the other side.

listitem.para: ooRexx using .NET. A Rexx program that requires net.cls gets the environment object &net;, the root of .NET's namespaces: going down by name reaches a namespace, then a type, whose messages are its static members and whose new makes an instance. Any .NET object is a instance, used with ordinary Rexx messages: a method call, a property read, or, with =, a property write.

.NET using ooRexx. A .NET program that references the assembly Rexx.Net (the NuGet package of that name) creates interpreter instances (), runs Rexx code, and uses any Rexx object as a , through C#'s dynamic or by name. It can give the Rexx code ADDRESS environments, functions, and its own standard streams.

Both at once. The two directions nest freely, on any thread: Rexx calls .NET, which calls back a Rexx method, which calls .NET again. A .NET object that goes to Rexx comes back as itself, and so does a Rexx object that goes to .NET. A Rexx class can extend a .NET class, so that .NET calls Rexx methods where it would call the overrides of a C# subclass (see ).

example.title: ooRexx using .NET
example.programlisting:
say .net~System~Math~Max(3, 7) sb = .net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new("Hello") sb~Append(", ")~Append("world") say sb~ToString sb~Length list = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<int>")~new list~Add(3); list~Add(1); list~Sort say list[0] list~Count -- a List counts from 0, as .NET says
::requires "net.cls"

example.title: .NET using ooRexx

section.title: Requirements
section.para: ooRexx 5.3.0 r13275 or later, 64-bit (a trunk build until 5.3.0 is released). The bridge uses only ooRexx's public native API: the interpreter needs no change, and the bridge is an extension package, as rxsock or BSF4ooRexx are. r13274 and r13275 fix crashes with command environments and threads (ooRexx bugs #2111 and #2112: adding an environment from .NET, or ADDRESS to one not yet known, while other threads run Rexx); r13270, a crash in SELECT CASE (#2114) that the installer and the samples could meet; on Linux, r13267 made calls from .NET into ooRexx much faster (#2106).

.NET 8 or later, 64-bit. The runtime is enough to run Rexx programs; the SDK only builds .NET programs. On Windows, the .NET Desktop Runtime adds Windows Forms, WPF and the rest of the desktop framework (see ). .NET Framework 4.x, the older Windows-only .NET, is not used.
The bridge runs on Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (Apple silicon).

section.title: The Parts of the Bridge

listitem.para: The Rexx side: the environment object &net; and the classes described in this book. A Rexx program uses the bridge with ::requires "net.cls".

varlistentry.term: librexxnet.so (librexxnet.dylib on macOS, rexxnet.dll on Windows)

listitem.para: The native half, an ooRexx external library that net.cls requires: it starts the .NET runtime when a program first uses &net;, and carries every request between the two sides.

The managed half, a .NET assembly, at the same time the other end of &net; (names, overloads, conversions, the handle table) and the API that .NET programs use to run Rexx code (). The runtime configuration names the .NET it needs (on Windows also Rexx.Net.core.runtimeconfig.json, see ).
A compatibility package: programs written for BSF4ooRexx's CLR.CLS run unchanged on it ().

section.para: The binary release installs them into an ooRexx installation (rexx install, or the Windows installer program), so that any program finds net.cls with no variables to set; the release's README.md explains it, and how to use the bridge without installing it. A .NET program gets the same files from the NuGet package Rexx.Net, which carries net.cls and CLR.CLS inside the assembly and the native library for each system ().

section.title: Which .NET
section.para: A program started by rexx starts the newest .NET installed, 8 or later, the first time it uses &net;; it stays until the process ends, and every interpreter instance of the process shares it. The .NET installation is the one the environment variable DOTNET_ROOT names, else the system's (where Microsoft's installers put it). A program started by .NET (a C# application, PowerShell) uses the .NET already running.

Three different things are called ".NET" on Windows. .NET Framework (4.x), the old Windows-only one that comes with Windows, is not used by the bridge. .NET (8, 10...; once ".NET Core") is, and Microsoft installs it in parts: the .NET Runtime (the base, Microsoft.NETCore.App), the .NET Desktop Runtime (the base plus the desktop framework, Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App: Windows Forms, WPF, System.Drawing, system sounds, the event log), the ASP.NET Core Runtime (web servers; not needed) and the SDK (everything, for building). Each comes for x64 and x86: a 64-bit ooRexx needs the x64 one; an x86 .NET is invisible to it.

On Windows the bridge adds the desktop framework when the newest .NET has it; when it does not, everything works but the desktop types (no .NET type "System.Windows.Forms.Form"). So install the .NET Desktop Runtime, x64 of your newest .NET, from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download. dotnet --list-runtimes shows what is installed: Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App must be there, with the same major version as the newest Microsoft.NETCore.App. has the rest of what differs between systems.

section.title: The Names in this Book
section.para: Rexx's names are those of net.cls: the environment object &net; (the instance of ), the classes NetObject, NetType, NetArray, NetEnum, NetNamespace, NetRef, NetTyped, NetHandler, NetEvent and NetCall, and the event thread's AbstractEventThread, NetEventThread and GUIMessage. .NET's names are those of the namespace Rexx.Net: RexxInterpreter, RexxObject and the classes of .

.NET's own types are named as .NET names them, by their full name (System.Text.StringBuilder), or by their C# alias where the bridge takes one (int for System.Int32). Generic types are written in C# syntax: System.Collections.Generic.List<int>.
The examples' outputs come from .NET 10 on Linux; where a value depends on the system (a path, a date, a version), the example avoids printing it.
